Cruachan Power Station is pump storage hydro that’s uses electricity from the grid to pump water to the upper reservior from Loch Awe, during periods of low demand. The process is reversed to generate electricity at periods of high demand and the site is currently being updated to increase capacity to 480 MW.
Basically a giant water battery hidden in a Scottish mountain, and it's been doing it since the 1960s.
This form of long term storage is required to balance the electricity network going forward and plans have been submitted to add 8-10GW of pump storage capacity over the next 10 years. All the new proposed sites located in Scotland.— at Cruachan Dam.

records.bodyText:
Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Middle East war. 
The UK has avoided the need for gas imports worth £5.9bn since the start of the Hormuz crisis as a result of record generation from wind and solar. 
While gas prices are surging to levels not seen since the 2022 energy crisis, the UK has been generating record amounts of power from wind and solar, up 14% year-on-year.
This unprecedented clean-power generation is directly cutting the need for gas-fired electricity, which is down by nearly 10% year-on-year in 2026 to date.
In total, wind and solar have generated a record 41% share of the UK’s electricity needs in 2026 to date, compared with 25% from gas.
The figure below shows that wind and solar has avoided the need for UK gas imports worth £5.9bn, since the outbreak of war between the US and Iran in February 2026.
These avoided gas imports would have required the UK to secure the equivalent of more than 100 additional tanker deliveries of liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The £1.3bn import saving in September 2026 to date is the result of record wind and solar output, at nearly 10 terawatt hours (TWh), combined with surging gas prices.
Wholesale gas prices in the UK have remained elevated ever since Russia cut off supplies to Europe in the wake of its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Gas averaged 90p per therm from 2023 until the start of this year, roughly three times above 2019 prices, before the Covid and Ukraine crises.
Since the outbreak of war in the Middle East in March, gas prices have climbed higher still, averaging 134p per therm or nearly four times the level seen in 2019.
In September 2026 to date, gas prices have averaged 189p per therm, reaching their highest level since the global energy crisis in 2022.

Batteries are good, no matter which side of the fence you sit on. Here is the latest update from Australian.
Australian NEM Batteries (Blue) are scaling up so fast, gas is being pushed out and capping renewable curtailment (Purple).
Context: Gas is a minor form of energy (GWh) in the NEM, despite having 12.7GW of capacity or 57% vs coal. Yet gas only produces 3.3% vs coal 49.7%. Why? Gas is at least 3x the cost.
Result: Average wholesale prices (what the retailers pay) have fallen consistently. 
On the 7th of September, grid batteries surpassed all peaking gas output (OCGT, Reciprocating, Steam) on a rolling 365 day basis.
In the next few days approximately a month since passing peaking gas (Brown), batteries will reach a new milestone >4,000 GWh rolling 365 days and overtake CCGT (Orange).
CCGT will also fall below the same point 4,000GWh for the first time since July 2001.
In the next 12 months, batteries will supply >6,000GWh, likely more than all gas.
Battery & Storage – 15x in 4 years.
Battery Discharging: 0.23M → 3.99M MWh (17x, YoY +216%).
Thanks to Andrew Klactus for this article and graph.

We've been waiting all day to post this.  The GMB General Secretary Gary Smith has laid into the Government in The Times.  That's no surprise to us as he has never been afraid of coming out in defence of his union members, formerly as  the Union's Scotland Secretary, where he would swing a wrecking ball with equal ease at the Westminster or the Scottish Government on the subjects of net zero and renewables. We have many of his quotes in our archives.
And he's still battling.
The reason we've had this in our pending tray is because we were waiting for confirmation from Kathryn Porter that there was no transcript or recording of a Labour Conference fringe debate - she, Dale Vince, Gary Smith and Amjad Bseisu of EnQuest,  Sadly, Kathryn doesn't believe that there was either.
So we are just contenting ourselves with the Times piece.
𝐒𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐙𝐞𝐫𝐨 𝐚𝐬 “𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐏𝟒𝟓𝐬” 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐚𝐢𝐝: “𝐖𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 [𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠] 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠-𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞.” 𝐇𝐞 𝐚𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝: “𝐈𝐭’𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐞. 𝐁𝐚𝐭𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐳𝐲.”
https://www.thetimes.com/.../union-leader-labour-energy...
'Labour’s energy policy is “crazy” and the department overseeing net zero is “basically the ministry for P45s”, one of Britain’s most powerful union leaders has said, as he urged ministers to approve new North Sea oil and gas projects or lose out on billions in investment. 
Gary Smith, the GMB general secretary, accused the government of relying on “sticking-plaster politics” while companies struggled with high energy costs and warned that rising energy bills would create a raft of fresh strikes across the public and private sector.
Smith described the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero as “basically the ministry for P45s” and said: “We are [using] sticking-plaster politics all the time.” He added: “It’s not credible. Batshit crazy.”
He warned a fresh rise in bills could trigger a new wave of strikes. He said: “The last time we had the spike in inflation, we had a spike in industrial unrest. That wasn’t driven by ideology. All that was driven by pure economics, housing economics.”
Smith’s intervention came as ministers prepared to decide on whether to approve drilling in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, off the coast of Scotland. 
The decisions rest with Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and it is widely expected that Jackdaw will be approved while the fate of Rosebank is less certain. However, industry sources believe both will go ahead, although the announcements will be delayed for political reasons as the Holborn & St Pancras by-election takes place next week.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in his speech to Labour Party conference in Liverpool this week that he would be “pragmatic” in relation to North Sea oil and gas “as we build a bridge to a clean energy future as we confront the climate crisis”. Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said a decision would be reached in the near future and the government was going through the evidence “piece by piece”.
In an interview with The Times, Smith warned rejecting either project would damage confidence in Britain as a place to invest.
He said: “If they do not do this, it will damage hugely the government’s credibility, and it will massively damage investment because that infrastructure, as I understand it, is ready to go — billions of investment. And if it does not now happen, who in their right mind is going to put money into this country?”
Smith went further and backed additional North Sea exploration beyond Rosebank and Jackdaw while Britain remained reliant on imported oil and gas.
The developments were previously approved under the Conservatives but consent was overturned by the courts in January last year, after judges ruled environmental assessments had failed to take account of the emissions created when the oil and gas was eventually burnt. Developers have since submitted fresh assessments and new government decisions are required before production can begin.
Asked whether ministers should permit more exploration, Smith said: “Yeah, absolutely. As long as we are importing, it is more energy-intensive and more carbon-intensive. It doesn’t make any sense in terms of environment and zero sense in terms of the economy.”
New figures this week showed domestic energy production fell by 5.8 per cent in the three months to June compared with the same period a year earlier. Total UK energy production in 2025 was at a record low and was 68 per cent below its 1999 peak.
Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, backed the sites. She told The Times: “We shouldn’t be letting go of one rope before we have got hold of another. Jackdaw is gas. We are going to be able to consume that, we need it and I think we need to go ahead and it should be done.
“We will run out of what’s in the North Sea,  but there’s a lot of time still left in there. We need the time to transition into the industries that we should transition into. 
“For me, of course I’m going to be jobs, jobs, jobs. But equally it’s about the security of the country as well. Until we have got the industries in place, we need to look at what we need. We’re almost cutting our nose off to spite our face. We are literally saying we are cutting this out when we’ve got absolutely nothing to replace it with.”
Smith said it did not make sense to focus on electricity when Britain’s homes were overwhelmingly reliant on gas.
He said: “Four times as much energy goes down the gas pipes as the electricity cables because we heat our homes with gas. If you want to transfer that energy usage, you’ve got to dig the cables up and make them four times bigger. You’re going to have to rewire all the way back to the transmission line.”
Meanwhile, households and businesses face fresh energy bill spikes driven by the war in Iran. 
The household price cap rose by 4 per cent to £1,723 for a typical dual-fuel household on Thursday, while Cornwall Insight has forecast a further 16 per cent rise in January to £1,999, an increase of £276. The consultancy has also estimated that business energy costs have risen by about 25 per cent since February.
Smith said: “When they say it’s going to be cheaper, I keep saying two things: when and how? Because it’s not.”
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero was contacted for comment.'

Key Details of the Ban
• The Rule: The Italian government approved a decree-law stopping new conventional ground-mounted photovoltaic (PV) systems on land zoned as agricultural. It also prevents expanding existing ground installations on farmland.
• The Goal: Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida stated the policy aims to stop the "wild installation" of solar panels and protect food production and productive rural land.
• The Constitutional Status: Italy’s Constitutional Court upheld the legitimacy of the regional and national agricultural land restrictions, ruling that protecting farmland does not violate EU law or the constitution.

CONON VALLEY HYDRO ELECTRIC SCHEME, VAICH DAM,
Williamson and Partners (engineers for North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board technical panel), 1957. Large turfed rubble dam with control tower to left (W) and 2 large spill towers near to upstream face. Mass rubble fill to downstream face with turf over; coursed random rubble to upstream face; concrete piers and walls to spill towers. Battered downstream face with concrete parapet to top. Additional concrete weirs and lined spillway channel adjacent to downstream face.
Vaich Dam is an excellent example of the innovation in dam design in response to local conditions and materials by the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board (NoSHEB) during their development of hydro electric schemes in the Highlands. It provides key storage capacity for Conon Valley hydro electric scheme, which is one of the major post-war hydro electric developments by the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board (NoSHEB). The dam is technically unusual, constructed predominantly from rubble fill, either side of a vertical concrete wall which is waterproof. As a consequence the dam cannot spill in the conventional manner as this would erode the downstream face, so large spill towers have been constructed adjacent to the upstream face, acting like large drains to allow water to spill into them and exit to the downstream side of the dam when water levels are high. The use of rubble fill instead of mass concrete saved a significant outlay in both time and money during the construction of the dam, which was consequently able to use tunnel spoil from the nearby shaft dug through to Glascarnoch Dam for the bulk of construction.
Conon Valley was one of a large number of schemes developed in Scotland by the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board (NoSHEB), formed after 1943 as a nationalised body to oversee the development of Scotland's resources for water power. The scheme played a key role in the realisation of the social agenda of NoSHEB by providing power to a remote community. Power generated on schemes in the southern Highlands, such as Tummel was exported via the grid to the central belt, the profit from which subsidised the provision of power to remote north Highland communities and stimulated economic regeneration. Under the leadership of eminent chairman Sir Tom Johnston the board undertook developments throughout Highland Scotland and his aspirations saw the development of schemes in locations such as Loch Dubh near Ullapool and Storr Lochs on Skye. Johnstone's social aspirations and wider wishes to reinvigorate the economy of the Highlands ensured that schemes in remote areas formed a key part of the NoSHEB development plan.
All of the developments carried out by NoSHEB were subject to parliamentary approval and objections on the grounds of scenic amenity were common. In order to meet these objections the board appointed a panel of architectural advisers which included Reginald Fairlie (1883-1952), James Shearer (1881-1962) and Harold Ogle Tarbolton (1869-1947), appointed in 1943. Initially the role of the panel was to adjudicate on competition entries for designs, but by 1947 it had become one of designers. The panel had little control over the functional form of the buildings, as they left this to engineers, but they did influence the appearance and the style of the designs. The rigid views on the roles of engineers and architects during the design process resulted in the development of a style which can be characterised as vernacular modernism. This style is characteristic of many NoSHEB buildings and is a direct product of the strict role which engineers and architects played in the design process and of the increasing desire to harmonise buildings with the landscape.
The design of Vaich Dam is typical of Williamson and Partners approach, with an innovative solution designed specifically to suit the requirements of a particular site. Their design allowed for the use of local materials and minimised the need for concrete thus saving significant amounts of time and labour in building a concrete batching plant and bringing materials to site. Williamson was a prominent engineer who specialised in the design of dams following his work on the Galloway Hydro Electric scheme, in the 1930s. He acted as one of the chief engineering advisors to NoSHEB and was the lead engineer for a number of schemes. Following his death in 1953 Williamson and Partners continued in the role as engineering advisors to NoSHEB building on the expertise developed during their long association with the development of hydro power.
Vaich Power Station is located at the end of the tunnel feeding Loch Glascarnoch.
